page: Amazon Web Services c8g.2xlarge is a compute-optimized instance powered by the custom AWS Graviton Neoverse-V2 processor. Built on the arm64 architecture, this instance features 8 dedicated physical cores and 8 vCPUs operating at a clock speed of 2.8 GHz with a 1:1 thread-to-core ratio. The processor is equipped with 64 KB of L1d cache, 2 MB of L2 cache, and 36 MB of L3 cache. It is provisioned with 16.0 GB of system memory, yielding a compute-focused ratio of 2.0 GB of RAM per core. The instance operates on the AWS Nitro hypervisor, includes a baseline network bandwidth of 4 Gbps, and does not feature local storage or integrated GPUs.

Performance benchmarks demonstrate strong single-core capabilities. The instance achieves a Geekbench single-core score of 1883.0 and a stress-ng single-core CPU performance of 1706.99, placing it in the top tier for single-threaded execution. This is further highlighted by strong single-threaded compression and decompression metrics, with gzip compression reaching 30.34 GB/sec and bzip3 decompression at 14.22 GB/sec. Memory bandwidth is also highly efficient, with uncached large-block read operations measured at 188.91 GB/sec. Multi-core execution remains balanced, yielding a Geekbench multi-core score of 10048.0 and a stress-ng multi-core score of 13647.2. However, cryptographic performance is a relative bottleneck, with the PassMark CPU encryption test scoring in the lower percentile at 1509.87.

Given its compute-centric hardware profile and high single-core efficiency, the c8g.2xlarge is well-suited for compute-bound workloads such as software compilation, text processing, and web serving. It delivers stable performance for lightweight language model inference, processing 553.43 tokens per second on small 135M models, though it struggles with larger models due to memory constraints. The arm64 architecture and dedicated core allocation provide a cost-efficient alternative to traditional x86 architectures, offering high resource density and predictable performance without hyperthreading overhead.
